content.intro: Learn database normalization in practice through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Database Normalization in Practice matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use database normalization in practice to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Repeating groups and first normal form, Partial dependencies and second normal form, Transitive dependencies and third normal form, Higher normal forms where appropriate. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Repeating groups and first normal form
items.text: Repeating groups and first normal form is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

content_blocks.code:
CREATE TEMP TABLE normalized_orders (order_id integer PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL);
CREATE TEMP TABLE normalized_order_items (order_id integer NOT NULL, product_id integer NOT NULL, quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id));
content_blocks.expected_output: Separate tables represent order-level facts and per-product line items; this avoids repeating order-level fields on every line.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate database normalization in practice using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic repeating groups and first normal form and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
